documents.title: WFH Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia 3rd Edition

chunks.content: Introduction Hemophilia A (hemoA) is an X-linked hereditary bleeding disorder resulting from a deficiency or dysfunction of factor VIII (FVIII). , The severity of hemoA is classified according to FVIII activity: mild (6%-40%), moderate (1%-5%), and severe (<1%), with severe cases frequently experiencing spontaneous bleeding episodes. Joints are commonly affected, leading to hemophilic arthropathy and the potential for long-term disability. , , , The standard therapeutic approach for severe hemoA involves prophylactic FVIII replacement to prevent bleeding and subsequent joint complications. , , However, ∼20% to 30% of patients develop FVIII inhibitors, which neutralize the efficacy of infused FVIII, making standard treatment ineffective. , FVIII inhibitors typically occur within 50 to 75 exposure days since patients start receiving FVIII injections. In such cases, bypassing agents such as activated factor VII or activated prothrombin complex concentrates are used as alternatives, although they are less effective than FVIII in patients without inhibitors. Risk factors for inhibitor development include patient age, intensity of FVIII exposure, F8 gene mutation, the patient’s immune background, and, arguably, the specific FVIII products used. , , , , Primary FVIII prophylaxis may reduce the initial intensity of FVIII exposure and thereby lower the risk of inhibitor formation. , Immune tolerance induction therapy remains the only established method for eliminating FVIII inhibitors; however, it is burdensome and costly owing to the need for prolonged, frequent, and high-dose FVIII infusions. The introduction of emicizumab, which mimics activated FVIII function, has fundamentally transformed the treatment landscape for patients with hemoA. Emicizumab, a humanized bispecific immunoglobulin G4 monoclonal antibody that bridges activated factor IX (FIX) and factor X (FX), partially restores hemostasis independently of FVIII and is unaffected by FVIII inhibitors. Clinical trials have demonstrated that emicizumab reduces bleeding episodes and improves outcomes for patients with hemoA, with or without FVIII inhibitors, across all age groups. , , , Approved by health authorities worldwide since 2017, emicizumab is administered subcutaneously every 1 to 4 weeks, providing a more convenient alternative to FVIII infusions. However, its binding affinity for activated FIX and FX is significantly lower than that of FVIII, and it does not fully meet coagulation demands during major trauma or surgery, necessitating supplementary FVIII administration (or activated factor VII for patients who already have an FVIII inhibitor) in such circumstances. Consequently, patients receiving emicizumab prophylaxis are typically exposed to FVIII only during breakthrough bleeds, trauma, or surgical procedures, situations historically associated with an increased risk of FVIII inhibitor development, , particularly in previously untreated patients (PUPs) before the emicizumab era. Whether emicizumab prophylaxis, especially in PUPs, would modify the risk of FVIII inhibitor formation remains unresolved, given that current clinical data do not elucidate the underlying immunological mechanisms. Some clinicians propose that the combined administration of emicizumab and prophylactic FVIII in PUPs may prevent the formation of inhibitors; however, whether this strategy is effective remains to be tested by clinical studies, which would be very challenging to conduct. To address this unresolved debate, we established a novel humanized mouse model to investigate the immunomodulatory role of emicizumab in the formation of FVIII inhibitors. Emicizumab specifically binds to human or primate FIX and FX, which limits the availability of appropriate animal models. The only published murine model supports only short-term observation, thereby precluding long-term efficacy assessments. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to generate a mouse model expressing human FIX (hFIX) and human FX (hFX), enabling extended evaluation and experimentation with emicizumab. Using this model, we further examined whether combining emicizumab with prophylactic FVIII reduces the risk of inhibitor development compared with on-demand FVIII treatment. We aimed to provide mechanistic insights to optimize hemophilia care and inform the design of future clinical studies. Materials and methods HemoA mice F8 knockout mice (hemoA), originally from H.H. Kazazian Jr, were bred and backcrossed with C57BL/6 for 10 generations. Male hemoA mice or wild-type littermates were used. Treatment groups and medications We conducted a 2-factor factorial experiment, with factors 1 (emicizumab vs no emicizumab) and 2 (on-demand FVIII vs FVIII prophylaxis), yielding 4 treatment groups ( ): (A) FVIII prophylaxis, (B) on-demand FVIII, (C) emicizumab prophylaxis with FVIII prophylaxis, and (D) emicizumab prophylaxis with on-demand FVIII (11-17 mice per group). Groups A and B were hemoA mice treated with FVIII weekly prophylaxis and on-demand FVIII, respectively, for 8 consecutive weeks. Groups C and D were hemoA mice injected with adeno-associated virus (AAV)-hFIX and AAV-hFX (4 × 10 12 vg/kg) at 4 weeks to establish the human hemoA (HemoA hFIX/hFX ) strain. They received emicizumab plus FVIII, given as prophylaxis (group C) or on demand (group D), following the same regimens as groups A and B. The FVIII used was efmoroctocog alfa (recombinant FVIII-Fc), administered via the retro-orbital route at 50 international units (IU)/kg weekly for 8 weeks, starting at 8 weeks of age.

B were hemoA mice treated with FVIII weekly prophylaxis and on-demand FVIII, respectively, for 8 consecutive weeks. Groups C and D were hemoA mice injected with adeno-associated virus (AAV)-hFIX and AAV-hFX (4 × 10 12 vg/kg) at 4 weeks to establish the human hemoA (HemoA hFIX/hFX ) strain. They received emicizumab plus FVIII, given as prophylaxis (group C) or on demand (group D), following the same regimens as groups A and B. The FVIII used was efmoroctocog alfa (recombinant FVIII-Fc), administered via the retro-orbital route at 50 international units (IU)/kg weekly for 8 weeks, starting at 8 weeks of age. Emicizumab was given subcutaneously at 3 mg/kg per week for 4 weeks (loading dose), then every 2 weeks as maintenance until study end. To mimic the on-demand FVIII condition, in groups B and D, FVIII was injected immediately after the right knee joint was injured. Mice were sacrificed 1 week after the final FVIII injection. Experimental procedures Blood samples were collected in 3.8% sodium citrate (volume-to-volume ratio, 9:1). Standard coagulation assays, including activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT); hFIX, hFX, and FVII levels; thrombin generation assay (TGA), and emicizumab concentration assay, were performed according to manufacturer protocols. FVIII inhibitors were assessed using a bovine chromogenic assay. Hemarthrosis was induced weekly for 8 weeks by needle puncture of the right knee joint, whereas the left knee remained uninjured and served as a control for joint outcome assessments. At the end of the study, joints were harvested for histology analysis, synovitis scoring, and microcomputed tomography (micro-CT). Detailed methods are presented in the . Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using the GraphPad Prism version 10.0.0 (GraphPad Software, Boston, MA, www.graphpad.com ) and the R 4.5.1 software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). In statistical testing, a 2-sided P ≤ .05 was considered statistically significant, and .05 < P ≤ .10 was regarded as marginal or borderline significance. In univariate analysis, differences in FVIII inhibitor titers among groups were visualized by box plots and examined using the Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test. Next, multivariate analysis was conducted by fitting linear regression models with factor 1 (emicizumab vs no emicizumab), factor 2 (on-demand FVIII vs FVIII prophylaxis), and their interaction term to estimate the main effects of these 2 factors and their interactive effect on the mean value of the FVIII inhibitor titers. Power transformation ( x q ) of the square root ( q = 0.5) was applied to the right-skewed continuous outcome variable, FVIII inhibitor titer, to make its distribution more symmetric ( ). The model-fitting techniques applied in our linear regression analysis are presented in the . All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Taiwan University College of Medicine Laboratory Animal Center. Results To assess the risk of FVIII inhibitor formation in patients treated with emicizumab, we used HemoA hfIX/hfX mice, which express hFIX and hFX, along with hemoA mice as the experimental models. Four experimental groups were created, as described in “Materials and methods” ( ). The levels of hFIX and hFX in our HemoA hfIX/hfX mice are crucial for evaluating emicizumab’s effect. We found that plasma levels of hFIX ( A) and hFX ( B) in HemoA hfIX/hfX reached 60.44 ± 12.69 IU/dL and 65.54 ± 9.75 IU/dL, respectively, at day 3 after AAV injection and gradually increased to 158.0 ± 57.9 IU/dL and 372.8 ± 170.7 IU/dL, over 12 weeks, ensuring sufficient substrate for emicizumab activity. To evaluate emicizumab’s ability to improve coagulation in these mice, we administered a single dose (3 mg/kg) and collected the plasma samples within 24 hours for aPTT, thrombin generation potential, and emicizumab concentration testing. We observed that emicizumab-treated HemoA hfIX/hfX mice showed fully shortened aPTT values within the normal range ( C). The emicizumab concentrations were 43.6 ± 3.6 μg/mL ( D). In addition, TGAs indicated partial restoration of coagulation function in the treated mice ( E; ). As control, we showed comparable FVII levels among groups ( ). These results demonstrate that emicizumab completely shortens aPTT and partially restores TGA curves in HemoA hfIX/hfX mice, supporting this model’s use for evaluating the in vivo coagulation effects of emicizumab. Experimental groups C and D comprised HemoA hfIX/hfX mice receiving emicizumab prophylaxis and weekly FVIII, without or with knee injury, respectively, for 8 weeks. As controls for the emicizumab-treated groups, groups A and B were hemoA mice receiving weekly FVIII without or with knee joint injury immediately before FVIII injection, respectively ( ). By the end of the experiments, all 55 mice, except 1 in group B, developed FVIII inhibitors, with all but 1 in group C being high-titer inhibitors. The median FVIII inhibitor titers were 109.4 Bethesda units (BU)/mL, 172.3 BU/mL, 28.7 BU/mL, and 43.6 BU/mL, for groups A, B, C, and D, respectively, as

HemoA hfIX/hfX mice receiving emicizumab prophylaxis and weekly FVIII, without or with knee injury, respectively, for 8 weeks. As controls for the emicizumab-treated groups, groups A and B were hemoA mice receiving weekly FVIII without or with knee joint injury immediately before FVIII injection, respectively ( ). By the end of the experiments, all 55 mice, except 1 in group B, developed FVIII inhibitors, with all but 1 in group C being high-titer inhibitors. The median FVIII inhibitor titers were 109.4 Bethesda units (BU)/mL, 172.3 BU/mL, 28.7 BU/mL, and 43.6 BU/mL, for groups A, B, C, and D, respectively, as shown by the 4 notched box plots in A. A statistical comparison of median FVIII inhibitor titers using the Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test showed significant differences among the 4 groups ( P = .0098). Series measurements of FVIII inhibitors in a subset of the mice are presented in C. Group B exhibited the fastest increase in FVIII inhibitor titer, whereas groups C and D showed much slower increases. Further analysis of the comparisons between the mean FVIII inhibitor titers at the 4 level combinations of factors 1 (emicizumab vs no emicizumab) and 2 (on-demand FVIII vs FVIII prophylaxis), as shown in the group mean plot ( B), reveals that emicizumab groups (factor 1) have lower FVIII inhibitor titers. In comparison, on-demand FVIII (factor 2) may provoke higher FVIII inhibitor titers. These 2 lines appeared unparallel; therefore, we tested the null hypothesis H0 that they are parallel vs the alternate hypothesis H1 that they are not, but we failed to reject the null, suggesting that there is no significant interactive effect of these 2 factors ( B). A multivariate analysis was conducted to estimate the main effects of these 2 factors on the mean FVIII inhibitor titers. Given that the distribution of FVIII inhibitor titers was severely skewed to the right ( ), we applied a square-root transformation ( x 0.5 ) to improve symmetry, thereby enabling more powerful statistical testing. Linear regression analysis revealed that mice receiving emicizumab had lower mean FVIII inhibitor titers (regression coefficient estimate = −5.7251; P = .0006) ( ). In parallel, on-demand FVIII (knee injury) increased the mean FVIII inhibitor titers with borderline significance (regression coefficient estimate = 2.9708; P = .0627) ( ). In the next part of this study, we conducted a new comparative analysis to assess the joint protection provided by emicizumab across 3 groups, all using HemoA hfIX/hfX mice and receiving weekly right knee injury for 8 consecutive weeks, as in the previous design. The first group received FVIII alone, the second received emicizumab alone, and the third received both emicizumab and FVIII (group D of ). The comparison among the 3 groups, as well as FVIII alone on hemoA (group B of ), enabled us to isolate and evaluate the protective effects of emicizumab monotherapy on articular structures after hemorrhagic events. We found that mice without emicizumab treatment demonstrated severe pathological manifestations, including extensive hematoma formation and significant hemosiderin deposition. Conversely, mice treated with emicizumab, whether or not FVIII was given, exhibited similarly improved outcomes, with only minimal scarring at the puncture site ( A). A comprehensive histological examination was subsequently performed to quantify joint damage severity and assess synovitis ( B). Hematoxylin and eosin staining of specimens from mice without emicizumab revealed substantial mononuclear cell and neutrophil infiltration, marked synovial hyperplasia, and mild neovascularization in the synovium and periarticular soft tissues. In addition, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, hemorrhage, synovial villus formation, and cartilage erosion were observed. In stark contrast, specimens from mice with emicizumab demonstrated significantly attenuated pathological changes, including only mild inflammatory cell infiltration, minimal synovial hyperplasia, and limited neovascularization. Consistently, F4/80 immunohistochemistry demonstrated marked macrophage infiltration in mice without emicizumab, but reduced infiltration in those with emicizumab ( ). Quantitative assessment of synovitis severity, using the validated scoring system developed by Valentino and Hakobyan, revealed a statistically significant reduction in synovial inflammation in the second and third groups (with emicizumab) compared with the first group (without emicizumab) or FVIII alone–treated hemoA mice (group B in ), as presented in C and . These findings demonstrate that emicizumab treatment provides substantial joint protection and significantly reduces synovial inflammation after hemorrhagic episodes in subjects with FVIII inhibitors. Using micro-CT and reconstructive imaging of the knee joints, the mice with emicizumab showed bone surfaces with mild roughness, minimal erosion, and sparse micropits, indicating preserved bone integrity. In contrast, the mice without emicizumab exhibited severely rough bone surfaces, characterized by extensive erosion, deep pits, and microcracks, indicating significant structural deterioration ( D). Further quantitative micro-CT analysis across the 3 groups revealed a significant reduction in bone mineral density (BMD) around the injured knees in the first group, which did not receive emicizumab ( E). Using micro-CT and reconstructive imaging of the knee joints, the mice with emicizumab showed bone surfaces with mild roughness, minimal erosion, and sparse micropits, indicating preserved bone integrity. In contrast, the mice without emicizumab exhibited severely rough bone surfaces, characterized by extensive erosion, deep pits, and microcracks, indicating significant structural deterioration ( D). Further quantitative micro-CT analysis across the 3 groups revealed a significant reduction in bone mineral density (BMD) around the injured knees in the first group, which did not receive emicizumab ( E). In the first group, BMD around the injured knee compared with the contralateral uninjured knee showed borderline significance (0.5100 ± 0.05090 vs 0.5586 ± 0.032 g/cm 3 ; P = .067). Other quantified bone markers, including bone volume fraction, trabecular thickness, and trabecular number of the femur and tibia, did not show differences among groups ( ). Discussion Emicizumab represents a revolutionary advance in the treatment of hemophilia. However, issues such as the risk of FVIII inhibitor development or long-term joint protection under emicizumab remain to be elucidated. Addressing these clinical issues related to emicizumab through clinical studies is expected to require a substantial number of patients and a considerable period of time. With a proper animal model, preclinical data can provide valuable insights and inform the design of clinical studies, potentially saving precious research resources. In this study, we present a newly developed mouse model that enables the evaluation of the effectiveness of emicizumab throughout the entire life span of mice, making it suitable for long-term experiments addressing clinical issues related to emicizumab. The total correction of aPTT and partial correction of TGA accurately reflect the expected clinical efficacy of emicizumab. The emicizumab plasma concentrations after a single injection were >30 μg/mL, which is generally considered an effective level. Our previous experiments with FIX knockin mice showed suboptimal transcription and translation levels of FIX, which may not be sufficient to sustain the function of emicizumab. Therefore, we chose AAV-based approaches to express hFIX and hFX in the mouse model rather than knockin approaches. We could not directly measure the function of hFIX and hFX because mouse FIX and FX are present. However, measurements of hFIX and hFX concentrations have shown sustained expression, and emicizumab has been effective throughout the experiment, indirectly confirming the existence of hFIX and hFX functions. Mouse FIX and FX did not interfere with the experimental processes. Some clinical trials aimed to explore the risk of FVIII inhibitor under emicizumab, but have not yet recruited sufficient patients to draw any conclusions. In our study, we wanted to address the same question with this novel mouse model. FVIII exposure, F8 mutation, genetic background, and bleeding conditions were well controlled within the experiment. However, our mice seemed to be prone to developing FVIII inhibitors, and almost all developed high-titer FVIII inhibitors by the end of the experiments. With such a high rate of inhibitor development, it is impossible to distinguish among the treatment groups. From this perspective, developing FVIII inhibitors is almost inevitable, regardless of how FVIII or emicizumab is given, for patients who inherently have a high risk of FVIII inhibitors. Although we could not demonstrate differences in the rate of FVIII inhibitor development, we examined FVIII inhibitor titers and observed some interesting patterns. The increase in inhibitor titers seems to be much slower in groups treated with emicizumab. By the end of the experiment, after 8 exposures to FVIII, inhibitor titers varied significantly among treatment groups. Mice receiving on-demand FVIII without emicizumab showed the fastest rise in titers and the highest levels at the end, whereas mice receiving emicizumab and prophylactic FVIII had the lowest titers. Further statistical analysis showed that emicizumab significantly reduced FVIII inhibitor titers ( P = .0006), whereas on-demand FVIII therapy tended to increase titers, with borderline significance ( P = .0627). Notably, the effect of emicizumab was greater than that of on-demand FVIII, indicating that recipients of emicizumab with on-demand FVIII have lower inhibitor titers than those on FVIII prophylaxis alone. From this perspective, our routine practice of administering emicizumab, which is exactly on-demand FVIII combined with emicizumab prophylaxis, might lead to lower FVIII inhibitor titers than FVIII prophylaxis without emicizumab, another common clinical approach. However, these findings pertain to inhibitor titers rather than the rate of inhibitor development. The presence of FVIII inhibitors has a greater clinical impact than the actual titers. Although these results are novel and intriguing, their implications for the development rate of FVIII inhibitors in clinical settings remain uncertain. Future studies could consider lower doses or reduced frequency of FVIII exposure to gain more insight into this matter. The presence of FVIII inhibitors has a greater clinical impact than the actual titers. Although these results are novel and intriguing, their implications for the development rate of FVIII inhibitors in clinical settings remain uncertain. Future studies could consider lower doses or reduced frequency of FVIII exposure to gain more insight into this matter. The final part of our study provides evidence of joint protection under emicizumab after repeated joint bleeds. The comparison among groups, using our HemoA hfIX/hfX mouse model with and without emicizumab, demonstrated a clear phenotypic distinction in appearance, histopathology, skeletal imaging, and BMD preservation, whereas whether FVIII was given did not significantly change joint outcomes. The groups receiving emicizumab had significantly less joint damage in almost all aspects. We deliberately created bleeding within the joints in the experiment; therefore, some degree of synovitis induced by the blood within the joint is expected, , even with emicizumab prophylaxis. To clarify, in our study, BMD was measured only around the specific joint; hence, the results reflect only bone loss directly related to hemarthrosis and subsequent arthropathy. We are aware that systemic osteoporosis is also an important issue in the hemophilia population, , but it is beyond the scope of this study. In conclusion, our newly developed HemoA hfIX/hfX mouse model is a valuable tool for exploring clinical questions about emicizumab. In HemoA hfIX/hfX mice, an effective emicizumab concentration fully normalized aPTT, partially improved thrombin generation, and protected against bleeding-induced arthropathy. We found that the rate of FVIII inhibitor development does not change significantly with emicizumab treatment, whether combined with on-demand or prophylactic FVIII replacement. However, the inhibitor titers and their rate of increase are reduced with emicizumab. This HemoA hfIX/hfX mouse model can serve as a platform for preclinical studies, providing insight into unanswered clinical questions about emicizumab and potentially supporting the design of future clinical studies.
